Associations between street light adaptation strategies and night-time road traffic collisions (Steinbach, 2015). 2.2.1.6 Spectral Content and Safety The purpose of roadway lighting is to increase the visibility of the roadway and the road environment. It complements lighting provided by vehicle headlamps on the forward roadway, as well as enhances the ability to detect off-axis hazards in the environment such as pedestrians, cyclists, and wildlife. The addition of roadway lighting has been shown in several scientific studies to reduce crash rates and increase safety as well as the feeling of safety. Elvik (1995) aggregated the results from 37 studies that compared lighted and unlit areas and determined that introducing roadway lighting should reduce fatal nighttime crashes by up to 65%. A study investigating the link between lighting level and night-to-day crash rate ratio found that there is both an impact of roadway lighting in the reduction of crashes but also a point where additional lighting does not further improve the safety performance of the roadway (Gibbons et al., 2014). Figure 5 shows the reduction in night-to-day crash rate ratio with increasing lighting levels. This impact is different based on the road class; Figure 6 shows the reduction in night-to-day crash 9 rate ratio for roads of differing classes. The dashed horizontal lines indicate where additional lighting does not improve the road safety. Figure 5. Night-to-day crash rate ratio to lighting level (Gibbons et al., 2014). Figure 6. Night-to-day crash rate ratio to lighting level for various road classes (Gibbons et al., 2014). Studies have also shown that additional roadway lighting results in an increase in visibility and detection distance of pedestrians and cyclists. Research to determine the use of adaptive lighting when traffic and pedestrian conflict is low found that a conventional lighting system could be dimmed to 40% of full power and still double the distance at which a pedestrian is visible 10 (Gibbons et al., 2015). These levels are not recommended when traffic is high, as full power roadway lighting mitigates headlamp glare, increases off-axis visibility, and provides more visibility for older drivers who require more light (Boyce, 2009). It has been determined that the presence of roadway lighting produces a significant increase in visibility attributable to the impact of increased surface luminance, which is said to reduce crash rates by 35% when increased by approximately1 cd/m2 (Scott, 1980). Several guides, both national and international, contain recommendations and guidelines for lighting implementations for all classifications of roadways.
